a: the slaves of God
p: Hermas's name for Christians all through the Similitudes. The Greek doulos means slave, not hired servant.
b: The Greek douloi tou theou is "slaves of God." The site renders doulos "slave" everywhere, because in Rome a doulos was owned property, not a paid servant, and many English Bibles soften it to "servant." Hermas knew the difference from the inside: the book opens with his being sold as a slave to a woman named Rhoda (1:1 (Vision 1.1.1)). In the Similitudes "slaves of God" is his ordinary name for believers, and the picture is filled out in 55, where a slave who does more than he is told is set free and made an heir.
orig: οἱ δοῦλοι τοῦ θεοῦ (hoi douloi tou theou)

a: live in a foreign land
p: The first parable makes believers foreigners in this world, with their true city far away.
b: The phrase epi xenēs katoikeite means "you live on foreign soil." Lake's English note here says the conflict between earthly and heavenly citizenship "is common in early Christian literature" and points to Hebrews 13:14: "We do not have a city here that remains. We are searching for the one that is coming" (Hebrews 13:14). The same thought stands in Hebrews 11:13-16 and 1 Peter 2:11 ("as resident aliens and temporary residents") and in Philippians 3:20. Hermas makes it into a little legal drama: two cities, two lords, two laws, and a choice which law to live by.
r: Hebrews 13:14; Hebrews 11:13-16; 1 Peter 2:11; Philippians 3:20; Epistle to Diognetus 5:5

a: costly estates
p: The Greek paratasseis usually means battle lines. Here it is the things a rich man lays out: estates and furnishings.
b: The usual meaning of paratasis in Greek is "a line of battle" or "arrangement" (so LSJ, which does not list the sense Hermas needs). Here it must mean what a wealthy man sets out for himself: estates, furnishings, the whole outfit of a comfortable life. Lake translates "costly establishments." The Plain English Translation says "costly estates" and, in 50:8, "estates," so the reader sees the same word return when Hermas tells the rich to spend these very things on the poor.

a: You foolish, double-minded, miserable man
p: Hermas's favorite fault, dipsychos, a person with two souls. The word first appears in James.
b: Dipsychos, literally "two-souled," is the site's "double-minded" (as James 1:8: "He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes"). Hermas uses the word and its verb more than any other early writer; Mandate 9 (39) is a whole lesson on it, written by another part of this book. Here the double-minded man is the one who wants both cities: a citizen of heaven who keeps buying land in this one. In Similitude 8 the half-dry sticks are the double-minded, "neither alive nor dead" (73:1).

a: the lord of this city
t: Who is the lord of this city?
p: Either the ruler of this world (the devil), or the earthly ruler, Rome, whose laws a Christian could not keep.
b: Hermas does not name him. Two readings are possible from the text. (1) He is the ruler of this present world, the power opposed to God, as in John 12:31; his "laws" are the world's ways, and the Christian who keeps God's law is "opposing" him (50:6). (2) He is the earthly power, the city of Rome and its emperor, whose laws and customs a Christian living in Rome could not fully obey, and who could seize property and expel. The story works on both levels: the believer's estates are hostages, and whoever owns much has much to lose when the master of this city turns against him.

a: Will you deny your law completely
p: In Rome, denial was a real choice: under pressure, a Christian could keep his estate by giving up his faith.
b: The verb aparneomai, "deny," is the word for renouncing Christ under pressure (Mark 14:72; Luke 12:9). Hermas ties it to property: the man with fields and houses has the most reason to deny. Similitude 8 returns to this: "because of their business they spoke evil against the Lord and denied him" (74:2), and some were rich and respected among the nations (75:1). In Rome a Christian could be denounced, and wealth could be confiscated; Hermas warns that holding on to it can cost the city that lasts.

a: with no one to insult you
p: Lake: the Greek may mean joy free of insult, or joy free of arrogance.
b: The adverb anybristōs is from hybris, insult or arrogance. Lake's English note says it "is either active or passive": joy where no one insults you (passive), or decorous joy, "unmixed with hybris" (active). The Plain English Translation takes the passive sense, which fits the picture of a man thrown out of a foreign city and coming home to his own, where no one can abuse him. Lake's text follows the Latin and Ethiopic here; the Athos manuscript reads two adverbs, "without insult and joyfully" (see the variant).

a: buy souls in distress
p: The rich are to buy people, not land: probably ransoming the oppressed and caring for widows and orphans.
b: "Buy souls in distress" is pointed. In a slave city it may mean ransoming slaves and captives, or paying the debts of the poor; the next words, "visit widows and orphans," echo James 1:27: "to visit orphans and widows in their trouble" (James 1:27), which Lake prints in his margin. The fields of the other city are people. Hermas, himself a former slave (1:1 (Vision 1.1.1)), may be thinking of the money that set slaves free.

a: This is why the Master made you rich
p: God made the rich rich so they could serve him with it, a thought that runs through the next parable too.
b: Here God is ho despotēs, "the Master" (the site's word for despotēs said of God). The thought is that wealth is a trust given for service. It is close to 1 Timothy 6:17-18: "Order those who are rich in the present age not to think highly of themselves ... They should do good, be rich in good works, give freely, and share what they have" (1 Timothy 6:17-18). Similitude 2 (51) works it out with the elm and the vine.

a: lavish spending
p: Polyteleia is extravagance. Hermas turns the vice into a virtue: spend lavishly, but on the poor.
b: LSJ gives polyteleia as "great expense, extravagance." Roman moralists used it for the luxury of the rich. Hermas keeps the word and turns it around: there is a lavish spending that is "good and holy" (50:10), the spending of the slaves of God on the poor, and a lavish spending "of the nations," which does them no good. "The nations" (ta ethnē) is the Bible's word for the non-Jewish peoples; for Hermas it means the pagan world around the church.

a: Do not counterfeit
p: The verb means to restamp or debase coins. Hermas may mean dishonest money dealing.
b: The Greek parecharassete comes from the language of the mint. LSJ gives "re-stamp," and especially "debase the currency." In this setting, a warning to people in business, it most likely means cheating with money, though it could be meant more widely, "do not falsify." Lake's English also says "do not counterfeit," and the Plain English Translation keeps the coin picture.

a: an elm and a vine
p: The parable assumes a vine trained up a living elm, a sight of the Italian countryside.
b: Hermas's parable assumes a sight his readers knew in the Italian countryside: a grapevine trained up a living elm tree, so that the tree holds the vine off the ground. The elm gives no grapes of its own; the vine on the ground gives poor fruit. Together they give a full crop. That is the whole parable.

a: the Shepherd appeared to me
p: The angel of repentance, who appeared in Vision 5 and gives the Mandates, now teaches by parables.
b: The Shepherd is the angel who appeared to Hermas in the dress of a shepherd in Vision 5 (25:1-3) and gave him the twelve Mandates. Hermas calls him kyrie, "sir": the same word as "Lord," so the site says "sir" where Hermas speaks to the angel and "the Lord" for God. In Similitude 6 two other shepherds appear (61-65); they are angels too, but the capital "Shepherd" is kept for this one, who gives the book its name.

a: a pattern
p: The Greek typos: a model or figure, the word behind "type."
b: The trees are set up eis typon, "as a typos." The site renders typos "figure" when it means a person who points forward to another (Romans 5:14), but here it means a model or object lesson for conduct, so "pattern." In 51:4 the same lesson is called a parabolē, "parable": the word that names this whole division of the book.

a: So this parable is set up
p: Hermas calls these lessons parables. The Latin version calls them similitudes, hence the name of the division.
b: The Greek is parabolē, "parable," the word the Gospels use for Jesus' stories. Lake prints the heading of this division as "The parables which he spoke with me," and notes that the Latin version translated the word similitudines, "hence the custom of quoting this section of the Shepherd as the 'Similitudes.'" The site keeps the old name for the division (Similitude 1-10) and says "parable" in the text. Unlike the Gospel parables, most of Hermas's are explained point by point by the angel.

a: His prayers for others and his praise
p: Enteuxis is prayer on someone's behalf. Exomologesis can be confession, but here likely thanksgiving or praise.
b: Enteuxis is a petition made to a superior, and in Christian Greek a prayer for others (1 Timothy 2:1; 4:5). Exomologēsis can mean confession of sin, which is how Lake and Crombie render it here, but LSJ also gives "confession of gratitude," and in the Greek Psalms the verb usually means to give thanks or praise. Since the poor man "thanks God" for the giver (51:6), the Plain English Translation reads it as praise. Later Latin writers used exomologesis for the public confession of penitents, a sense that may be in view in a book about repentance.
orig: τὴν ἔντευξιν καὶ τὴν ἐξομολόγησιν (tēn enteuxin kai tēn exomologēsin)

a: the poor man is rich in prayer
p: The rich are poor toward God and the poor are rich, as in James and the Gospels.
b: The reversal echoes James 2:5 ("the poor, poor as the world counts it, whom God picked out to be rich in faith") and Jesus' warning about the one who "is not rich toward God" (Luke 12:21). Hermas makes it a partnership rather than a rebuke: each has what the other lacks. The poor man's prayer "has great power with God" because God hears the poor (Psalm 34:6).

a: without hesitating
p: The opposite of double-mindedness: the giver does not stop to wonder whether to give.
b: Adistaktōs means "without doubting, without hesitating." The same idea is in the Didache: "You must not hesitate to give" (Didache 4:7) and in Mandate 2, where Hermas is told to give to all without asking who deserves it (27:4-6 (Mandate 2.4-6)). For Hermas, hesitation is a form of the double mind.

a: make their wealth complete
p: Lake: the verb means filling up a lack. The word "prayers" here is a modern guess; the Greek manuscript has "souls."
b: The verb plērophoreō means to bring to full measure (LSJ); Lake's English note says "the idea ... is that of filling up that which is lacking." The rich man lacks prayer, the poor man lacks bread, and each fills up the other's lack. Whose prayers or souls are "completed" is a text problem: see the variant on this phrase.

a: written in the books of the living
p: The heavenly register of the righteous, from the Psalms, Daniel and Revelation.
b: The image of a heavenly book of names is old: "Let them be wiped out of the scroll of life, and not be written down with the righteous" (Psalm 69:28); "everyone found written in the scroll" (Daniel 12:1); "I will never erase his name from the book of life" (Revelation 3:5). Hermas uses the plural, "books," as Daniel 7:10 does ("books were opened"). The phrase returns in Hermas's Visions and Mandates, where the forgiven are written in the books of life.
r: Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Daniel 7:10; Revelation 3:5; Philippians 4:3; Exodus 32:32

a: this world is winter for the righteous
p: In winter dead and living trees look the same. Only summer shows which ones live.
b: Similitudes 3 and 4 are one picture told twice. In winter a dead tree and a sleeping one are both bare. In summer the living tree leafs out and bears fruit, and the dead one is plainly dead. "This world" (ho aiōn houtos, literally "this age") and "the age that is coming" (53:2) are the two ages of Jewish and Christian hope (Matthew 12:32; Ephesians 1:21); the site says "this world" for the present age, as Lake does. The lesson is the patience of the wheat and the weeds: the church cannot yet tell the righteous from sinners for sure (Matthew 13:24-30).

a: when the Lord's mercy shines out
p: The day that shows everyone for what they are is called the shining of the Lord's mercy.
b: Hermas does not say "when the Lord comes to judge" but "when the Lord's mercy shines out" (epilampsē to eleos). For the righteous the last day is summer and mercy; for sinners and the nations it is winter and fire (53:4). The mixed picture matches the New Testament, where the same day is both hope and judgment (Titus 2:13; 2 Thessalonians 1:6-10). In Hermas it fits the theme of the whole book: the time of repentance is now, before that light shows each tree for what it is.

a: They will be burned up like wood
p: Fruitless trees burned: the picture of John the Baptist and of John 15.
b: The fruitless tree in the fire is a Gospel picture: John the Baptist's "Any tree that fails to produce good fruit is being cut down and thrown into a fire" (Matthew 3:10) and Jesus' branch that "dries up" and is thrown into the fire (John 15:6). Hermas gives two reasons for the burning. Sinners burn "because they sinned and did not repent"; the nations burn "because they did not know the one who created them" (compare Romans 1:20-21). In Similitude 8 the dry sticks are again the ones with least hope (72:4).

a: Stay out of too many dealings
p: Hermas warns traders that many deals mean many sins, and allows one business, done with a pure mind.
b: The word praxeis means doings, affairs, business deals. Hermas knew this from inside: the old woman of the Visions tells him that because of his household's sins he was "corrupted by the affairs of everyday life" (3:1 (Vision 1.3.1)). Here he does not forbid business but warns against having too much of it: "if someone works at one business, he can serve the Lord too" (53:7). Compare 2 Timothy 2:4, "No one serving in the army gets tangled up in the business of everyday life" (2 Timothy 2:4), and Similitude 8's people "tangled up in business" (74:1).

a: I am keeping a station
p: Hermas uses a Latin army word, statio, for a fast day. Lake: Tertullian explains it from military duty.
b: Hermas writes statiōna echō, "I have a station," borrowing the Latin statio, a soldier's post or watch. Lake's English note says the word "is not found elsewhere in Greek writers but is used in Latin writers in the sense of a fixed time for fasting," citing Tertullian, On Prayer 19 and On Fasting 1 and 10, and Tertullian's own explanation: "statio de militari exemplo nomen accepit, nam et militia dei sumus," which in the site's own translation says that the station takes its name from the army, "for we too are God's soldiers." The Shepherd asks what the word means, which suggests it was a church word in Rome before it was common speech.

a: sitting on a mountain
p: Hermas goes out of the city at dawn to fast and pray, as he went into the country in the Visions.
b: Hermas's visions often begin when he is alone in the country near Rome, walking or praying (1:3; 5:1; 22:2). Here he sits on a mountain at dawn to keep his fast. Mountains were places of prayer in the Bible (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19:8; Luke 6:12), and the Shepherd's "why have you come here so early?" sets up the lesson that the place and the hour are not what make a fast.

a: You people do not know how to fast to the Lord
p: Like Isaiah 58, the angel says that going without food is no fast without righteousness.
b: The Shepherd's speech follows the line of Isaiah 58: "Is a fast like this the one I would choose ... Is this not the fasting I choose: to unlock the fetters of wickedness" (Isaiah 58:5-6), and Zechariah 7:5-10. The Shepherd shifts to the plural, "you people," so the criticism is of a common practice, not only Hermas's. He does not abolish the fast (in 56:5-7 he gives rules for it) but says that a fast without obedience is "empty" and "useless." Barnabas 3 quotes Isaiah 58 for the same point.
r: Isaiah 58:3-7; Zechariah 7:5-10; Joel 2:12-13; Epistle of Barnabas 3:1-5; Matthew 6:16-18

a: Keep his commandments
p: The real fast is a life of obedience. Lake's margin points to Jesus: "obey the commandments."
b: Lake prints Matthew 19:17 in the margin: "But if you want to enter into life, obey the commandments" (Matthew 19:17). The "great fast" is simply the life the Mandates described: no evil, a pure heart, the commandments kept, no evil desire, faith in God, fear of him. "You will live to God" is Hermas's refrain for salvation (it closes many Mandates and Similitude 8, 77:4).

a: A man had a field and many slaves
p: A master, a vineyard, a trip abroad, a slave and a beloved son: the furniture of Jesus' parables, rearranged.
b: Every piece of this story is in the Gospels: the vineyard planted by a man who "left the country" (Mark 12:1), the "dearly loved son" who is heir (Mark 12:6; Matthew 21:38), the slaves left in charge until the master comes back (Matthew 24:45-51; 25:14-30), the slave who did only what he was told (Luke 17:7-10). But Hermas's story goes the other way from the Gospels' tenants: the slave does more than he is told, and instead of the heir being killed, the slave is made a fellow heir with the son. The angel will say the slave is the Son of God (58:2).

a: put stakes in it
p: Vines in rows were tied to stakes or a frame. The slave is ordered to stake them and nothing more.
b: The verb charakoō means to fit with stakes (charax), the wooden props that held up the vines. In 58:3 the stakes are the angels who hold God's people together. The order is limited on purpose: stake the vines and do nothing else. What matters is that the slave goes beyond it and digs and weeds.

a: I will set you free
p: In Rome a master could free a trusted slave. Hermas himself had been one.
b: Roman masters often freed trusted slaves, and a freedman could rise high. To be made an heir as well, together with the master's own son, goes far beyond freedom. Hermas, sold as a slave in his youth (1:1 (Vision 1.1.1)), tells this part of the story with care: freedom is the promised reward, sonship the surprise.

a: Then the slave's master went away on a journey abroad
p: Lake thinks something is missing here. The Latin puts the journey first: the master was going abroad, then chose a slave.
b: Lake's footnote: "There is probably something missing in the text"; the Vulgate Latin (L1) reads deinde peregre profectus elegit servum, "then, setting out abroad, he chose a slave," and the Palatine Latin and Ethiopic "paraphrase the whole, but insert the phrase peregre afuturus," "being about to be abroad." In the Athos manuscript the trip comes only at the end of the verse. Either way the master is absent while the slave works, which the explanation calls "the time that is left until his coming" (58:3).
orig: ἐξῆλθε δὲ ὁ δεσπότης τοῦ δούλου εἰς τὴν ἀποδημίαν

a: his beloved son, who was his heir
p: The words of the Gospel parable of the vineyard: the son is "beloved" and "heir."
b: "Beloved son" (huios agapētos) is what the voice from heaven calls Jesus (Mark 1:11; 9:7) and what the vineyard owner calls his son (Mark 12:6). "Heir" (klēronomos) is the word of Mark 12:7 and Hebrews 1:2 ("God appointed him heir of all things"). Hermas's parable has both a son and a slave who is like a son. The angel explains the slave (58:2) but, as Lake's English note says, "the Son in the parable ... remains unexplained."

a: the friends who were his advisers
p: A Roman great man had a council of friends. In the explanation they are the first-created angels.
b: A Roman head of a household or magistrate made decisions with a consilium, a council of friends; Hermas's Greek symbouloi, "advisers," is the same idea. In the explanation the friends are "the holy angels who were created first" (58:3), the six who in Vision 3 build the tower (12:1 (Vision 3.4.1)). God consulting a council of angels recalls the heavenly council of 1 Kings 22:19-22 and Job 1-2.
orig: φίλους, οὓς εἶχε συμβούλους (philous, hous eiche symboulous)

a: an heir together with my son
p: Paul's word for believers: heirs of God, sharing the inheritance with Christ.
b: The Greek synklēronomos, "fellow heir," is Paul's word: "We are heirs of God, sharing the inheritance with Christ" (Romans 8:17), and Galatians 4:7: "You are a son. And since you are a son, you are also an heir, through God" (Galatians 4:7). In Hermas the parable's slave who becomes co-heir with the son is, at one level, the faithful believer who does more than is commanded; in the explanation (59:5-7) he is the "flesh" that served the Holy Spirit and was made the Spirit's partner.

a: shared the rest with his fellow slaves
p: Masters sent portions from a feast to favored dependents. The slave shares his.
b: Sending portions of food from a banquet to friends, clients and favored slaves was a Roman custom (and a biblical one: Nehemiah 8:10; Esther 9:19). The slave keeps what is enough and gives away the rest, which is the point of the fast that follows: eat bread and water and give the cost of the meal away (56:7). In the explanation the dishes are "the commandments he gave his people through his Son" (58:3).

a: if you do some good beyond what God commands
p: This verse was long cited in arguments over "works of supererogation": good done beyond what God requires.
b: The Greek is ektos tēs entolēs tou theou, "outside God's commandment." The doer wins "more glory" and "higher honor." Philip Schaff, a Reformed church historian, says of the book as a whole, without citing a verse, that Hermas "teaches not only the merit, but the supererogatory merit of good works." This verse is the plainest place for that judgment (the site's reading). Whether a person can do more than God requires is a question the churches answer differently; the site sets their answers side by side in the "Where Christians differ" card at Luke 17:10 ("When you have done all you were ordered to do, say, 'We are useless slaves'"). Hermas's own example is modest: giving away the cost of the fast-day meal.
orig: ἐκτὸς τῆς ἐντολῆς τοῦ θεοῦ (ektos tēs entolēs tou theou)

a: these services
p: Leitourgia, the word behind "liturgy": here acts of devotion like the fast and its gift.
b: Leitourgia is the site's "service" (gloss: public worship service, the word behind "liturgy"). In Athens it was a public duty a rich citizen paid for; in the Greek Bible it is temple service. Hermas uses it for the fast and its gift (56:3, 56:8) and for Hermas's serving the Lord (66:6): voluntary acts of devotion offered to God.

a: When you have carried out what is written
p: Probably the rules just given (56:6), not a passage of Scripture.
b: Synteleseas ta gegrammena, "having completed the things written," most likely refers to the instructions just given in 56:6 (guard against evil words and desires), which Hermas was told to write down (as in 25:5-7 (Vision 5.5-7)). It is not a quotation formula; Hermas names no written Scripture here.

a: nothing but bread and water
p: The fast is not a total fast but a day on bread and water, with the saved cost given away.
b: The fast Hermas is taught is a day of bread and water, then a reckoning: add up what the day's food would have cost and give it to "a widow or an orphan or someone in need." Isaiah 58:7 already joins fasting and feeding the hungry ("to break your bread for the hungry"). The site's Isaiah 56-66 chapter pages mention this passage as an early Christian use of Isaiah's teaching.

a: your sacrifice will be acceptable to God
p: Lake's margin points to Philippians 4:18: a gift to others is a sacrifice God accepts.
b: Lake prints Philippians 4:18 in the margin, where Paul calls the Philippians' gift "a soothing smell, a sacrifice that God accepts and that pleases him" (Philippians 4:18), and Sirach 35 (the Latin numbering; Swete's 32), on the sacrifice of the righteous. Hermas's fast is "written down" (engraphos) in heaven, like the books of 51:9. Compare Hebrews 13:16: "Those are the kinds of sacrifices God takes pleasure in" (Hebrews 13:16).

a: you and your children and your whole household
p: The household is the unit of faith. Hermas's household comes back in Similitude 7.
b: The fast is for Hermas's whole household: his children, and probably slaves and dependents. In the Visions his family had sinned and was called to repent (3:1-4:3 (Vision 1.3-2.3)); in Similitude 7 (66) Hermas is afflicted because of his household's sins. Roman households, and Roman churches that met in them (Romans 16:5), were the place where faith was taught and practiced.

a: You are far too bold with your questions
p: The angel teases Hermas for his questions, but answers them, as angels do in Daniel and 4 Ezra.
b: The seer who keeps asking and the guide who first refuses and then explains is a regular feature of Jewish apocalypses: Daniel asks the angel (Daniel 7:16; 12:8), and Ezra presses the angel Uriel again and again in 4 Ezra 4-5. Hermas is "bold" (authadēs, self-willed) and later "sly" (panourgos, 58:1), but his persistence is rewarded "so that you can make it known to everyone" (58:1). The book is written to be passed on.

a: asks him for understanding and receives it
p: Like James 1:5: God gives to all who ask, without scolding.
b: "If any of you is short of wisdom, let him ask God for it. God gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding, and it will be given to him" (James 1:5). Hermas is the early writer closest to James, and the pairing is plain here: the one who has the Lord in his heart asks and receives, the double-minded hesitate (distazousin, compare James 1:6-8). The angel's point is that parables are opened by prayer, not only by explanation.

a: the holy angel
p: An angel who strengthened Hermas: probably the glorious angel who sent the Shepherd.
b: Hermas has been "made strong by the holy angel" and has received prayer "from him." The Shepherd was sent by "the most revered angel" (25:2 (Vision 5.2)), and a "glorious angel" gives orders about Hermas (66:1, 66:5); in 69:3 the glorious angel of Similitude 8 is named as Michael, and in Similitude 9 a "glorious man" is the Son of God (89). Whether these are one figure, and whether that figure is Christ, is debated: see the chapter page of 69.

a: sly and bold
p: Panourgos usually means crafty or unscrupulous. Here it is the angel's mock-scolding of Hermas.
b: Panourgos is literally "ready to do anything," usually in a bad sense: crafty, knavish (Paul uses it of himself as his opponents saw him, 2 Corinthians 12:16). The Shepherd uses it half in jest: Hermas is clever at getting answers out of him. The Plain English Translation says "sly" to keep the edge.

a: The field is this world
p: The opening of Jesus' explanation of the weeds (Matthew 13:38), which Lake prints in the margin.
b: Lake's margin points to Matthew 13:38: "The field is the world" (Matthew 13:38), from Jesus' own explanation of a parable in the same point-by-point style. Hermas's explanations follow that model: field, lord, slave, vines, stakes, weeds, dishes, friends, journey, each given its meaning. The weeds here are not people, as in Matthew, but "the lawless acts of God's slaves" (58:3), cleared away by the slave's toil.

a: the one who created all things, put them in order and gave them power
p: Lake's margin: Ephesians 3:9, "the creator of all things," and the Greek Psalm 68:28 on God's strength.
b: The three verbs (ktisas, created; apartisas, completed or put in order; dynamōsas, gave power) are Hermas's standing description of God (Mandate 1, 26:1, and 66:4). Lake prints Ephesians 3:9 in the margin, "God, the creator of all things" (Ephesians 3:9), and Psalm 68:28 in its Greek form, which asks God to "strengthen" what he has done for us.

a: The slave is the Son of God
t: The slave is the Son of God
p: The surprising heart of the parable. The Latin version adds: "and the Son is the Holy Spirit."
b: Hermas himself is startled (58:5): why would the Son of God be a slave in a story? The answer in 59 is that the slave stands for the Son's work, toiling to cleanse the people's sins, while his true place is "great authority and lordship" (59:1). One Latin version adds here "but the Son is the Holy Spirit" (see the variant), which Lake compares with 78:1 (Similitude 9.1.1), "that Spirit is the Son of God." How Hermas joins the Son, the Spirit and the "flesh" is the most debated question in the book: see the chapter page of 59.
orig: ὁ δὲ δοῦλος ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν

a: the holy angels who were created first
p: Six angels, created first, advise God and build the tower. Hermas never names them.
b: In Vision 3 the tower is built by "six young men" who are "the holy angels of God who were created first" (12:1 (Vision 3.4.1)); in Similitude 9 six men come with the glorious man (82). Jewish and Christian writings also speak of a small group of chief angels: seven in Tobit 12:15 and Revelation 8:2, and seven named in 1 Enoch 20:2-8. Hermas's six, with the glorious one above them, may reflect such a tradition; he never gives their names.

a: the time that is left until his coming
p: The master's absence is the church's present time, before the Lord's return.
b: Parousia, "coming," is the New Testament word for Christ's return (Matthew 24:3; 1 Thessalonians 4:15). In the parable it is the master's coming, so it may be God's coming or the Son's. Hermas expects it, but his main concern is what believers do while they wait, as in the Gospel parables of the absent master (Matthew 24:45-51; Mark 13:34-37). The "time that is left" is the time for repentance that the whole book announces.
orig: εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν αὐτοῦ (eis tēn parousian autou)

a: in the form of a slave
p: Hermas's question sounds like Philippians 2:7, but his words are not Paul's.
b: Hermas asks why the Son is set eis doulou tropon, "in a slave's manner." Paul's hymn says Christ "emptied himself, taking a slave's form" (Philippians 2:7), with morphē, "form," not tropos. Whether Hermas knew Philippians is not certain from this wording. The answer he receives goes a different way from Paul's: the Son is not really in a slave's place but "in great authority" (59:1), and the one who serves as a slave is "the flesh" (59:5-6).

a: he himself cleansed their sins
p: Hermas's one statement of what the Son did for sins, in the words of Hebrews 1:3.
b: "He himself cleansed their sins, working hard and bearing much toil." Hebrews 1:3 says the Son "had made a cleansing for sins" (Hebrews 1:3; Greek katharismon tōn hamartiōn poiēsamenos). Hermas does not mention the cross; the Son's "toil" is the digging and weeding of the vineyard. Readers differ on how much to read in: Schaff says Christ is "nowhere named" in the book, while the toil and the cleansing of sins are often taken as Hermas's way of speaking of the passion.

a: the Son put the angels over them to guard them
p: The angels who guard God's people serve under the Son.
b: The stakes of the parable are the angels (58:3), and here the Son appoints them. Guardian angels of nations and of God's people are an old Jewish idea (Deuteronomy 32:8 in the Greek; Daniel 10:13, 21, where Michael is Israel's "prince"). Hermas places the angels under the Son, much as Hebrews 1:4-14 sets the Son above the angels. In Similitude 8 the angel over this people is Michael (69:3).

a: the paths of life
t: Paths of life and the law
p: Psalm 16:11 in Lake's margin, and John's language of the command the Son received from the Father.
b: "The paths of life" echoes Psalm 16:11, "You let me know the path of life" (Psalm 16:11), which Lake prints in the margin with Proverbs. "The law that he received from his Father" recalls Jesus' words in John: "This is the command I received from my Father" (John 10:18), and John 12:49 and 15:10, also in Lake's margin. For Hermas the Christian life is a "law" given through the Son; in 69:2 the law is the Son himself.

a: The Holy Spirit, who existed before, who created all creation
p: The verse most argued over in Hermas: the Spirit who made all things lives in a chosen flesh.
b: Hermas names the Holy Spirit, not the Son or the Word, as the one who existed before and "created all creation," and says God made this Spirit live "in flesh that he wanted." The New Testament says creation came through the Son (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). Lake's English note on 59:6 explains the flesh as "the human being" in whom "the Spirit had been incarnate," raised to be companion "of the Father and of the Son who is the Spirit." Harnack reads the passage as adoptionist; Chapman (Catholic Encyclopedia) writes that "it has been thought with some reason that he did not distinguish the Son from the Holy Ghost," but that "his words are not clear," and his ideas "may have been rather misty and confused than definitely erroneous." The readings are set out on the chapter page. The Plain English Translation says "who" for the Greek neuter, as English does for the Holy Spirit. "That he wanted" (ēbouleto, Lake "which he willed") is God's purpose; the different verb of 59:6, heilato, is "chose."
orig: τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τὸ προόν, τὸ κτίσαν πᾶσαν τὴν κτίσιν

a: served the Spirit well as a slave
p: Here the slave of the parable turns out to be the flesh that served the Spirit.
b: The verb edouleuse, "served as a slave," ties this verse to the parable. In 58:2 the slave was "the Son of God"; here the one who serves as a slave is "this flesh." Hermas seems to use "Son" for the whole person in whom the Spirit lived, and "flesh" for the human side that obeyed. The parable does not map neatly onto a single figure, which is one reason his meaning is debated (see the chapter page).

a: did not defile the Spirit in any way
p: The bare Greek "the spirit" points back to the Holy Spirit just named, so the site capitalizes it, through 60:4.
b: In 59:5-7 Hermas writes "the Holy Spirit" (to pneuma to hagion) five times and the bare "the spirit" (to pneuma) four times. Each bare form refers back to the Holy Spirit of the same sentence, so the Plain English Translation writes "the Spirit." Greek has no capitals to decide this; the capital follows the sense. The site keeps the capital through the next chapter. In 60:1 "the Spirit that lives in it" uses the verb of 59:7 (the Holy Spirit "has lived" in the flesh), and 60:2 names "the Holy Spirit" outright. In 60:4, "your flesh or the Spirit," the pair "belong together," as flesh and Holy Spirit do in 60:2. Lake's English writes "spirit" in lower case in 59:5 and 60:1, and 60:1 and 60:4 can be read of the believer's own spirit: then Hermas would be saying that body and soul are kept pure or defiled together.

a: he chose it as a partner with the Holy Spirit
p: The obedient flesh is chosen as the Spirit's partner: Harnack calls this adoption; others an exaltation after the resurrection.
b: Heilato koinōnon, "he chose (it as) partner." Lake's note: "the flesh (i.e. the human being), in which the Spirit had been incarnate, was elevated to be the companion, for the future, of the Father and of the Son who is the Spirit." Harnack takes this as the heart of an "Adoptian" Christology: the man chosen by God who "did more than he was commanded" was "adopted as a son and exalted." Compare the New Testament's language of exaltation after obedience (Philippians 2:9; Acts 2:36; Hebrews 5:8-9), where the one exalted had existed before (Philippians 2:6). On "pleased him," see the variant.

a: all flesh in which the Holy Spirit has lived will receive a reward
t: From the Son to every believer
p: What happened to that flesh will happen to every believer's flesh that stays pure.
b: The explanation widens at once: "all flesh" in which the Holy Spirit has lived will be rewarded if it is "undefiled and spotless." Harnack notes that this parallel between Jesus and "all believers who have the Spirit" is clear in Hermas, and calls 59:5-7 the most important passage for it. For Hermas the purpose of the parable is moral: the next chapter turns straight to Hermas's own flesh (60:1). Compare 1 Corinthians 6:19, "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (1 Corinthians 6:19).

a: this flesh of yours is perishable
p: Lake: aimed at teachers who said the body did not matter. The church held to purity and the resurrection of the flesh.
b: Lake's English note: "This is directed against the Gnostic tendency to divide flesh and spirit, and to regard the acts of the flesh as unimportant. Against this the church insisted on purity of life now, and on the hope of a resurrection of the flesh hereafter." Some second-century teachers argued that only the spirit is saved, so what the body does is indifferent. Hermas answers that flesh and spirit "belong together" (60:4). Compare 1 Corinthians 6:13-20 and 15:42-44.

a: the earlier sins of ignorance
p: Sins committed before the message was heard are left to God's healing, on condition of purity from now on.
b: Hermas asks the book's constant question: what about sins already done? The answer is cautious. Healing for "sins of ignorance" (agnoēmata) belongs to God alone, "if from now on" the person keeps pure. The same pattern runs through the book: one new chance, offered now, for sins committed before the announcement (6:4-8 (Vision 2.2.4-8); 31:6). Compare Acts 17:30 ("God has looked past those times of not knowing") and Hebrews 9:7, where the high priest offers for the people's sins of ignorance.
orig: περὶ τῶν προτέρων ἀγνοημάτων (peri tōn proterōn agnoēmatōn)

a: for all authority is his
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 28:18, though there the authority is given to Jesus.
b: Lake's margin points to Matthew 28:18: "I have been given all authority, in heaven and on earth" (Matthew 28:18). In Hermas the authority is God's. One Latin text that Lake cites as a variant (59:3) says the Son received "all authority from his Father"; the two passages together echo the Gospel line.

a: Put on faith in the Lord
p: Hermas often speaks of putting on and taking off virtues and vices like clothes.
b: "Put on faith" (endysai tēn pistin), "throw off the evils" (61:4), "put on every virtue" (61:4), "clothed in great foolishness" (65:3), "put on great pride" (75:1): Hermas thinks of character as clothing. The image is Paul's (Romans 13:12-14; Ephesians 4:22-24; Colossians 3:9-12) and the Psalms' (Psalm 132:9). In Similitude 8 those who enter the tower receive white clothing (68:3).

a: These commandments are good for those who are going to repent
p: The Mandates are a rule of life for those who repent. Without it, repentance is empty.
b: Here the Shepherd states the plan of the book. Lake's introduction puts it this way: "in the Mandates the life required from the penitent is explained, and in the Similitudes the working and theological doctrine of repentance is developed." Repentance for Hermas is not only sorrow but a changed life kept up "from now on" (61:4: "add no more to your sins"). James 2:17, "If it has no works, it is dead in itself" (James 2:17), says something similar about faith.

a: a young shepherd dressed in a suit of clothes the color of saffron
p: A young, cheerful shepherd in yellow: the angel of luxury, attractive as pleasure is.
b: The young shepherd's clothes are saffron-yellow (krokōdēs), a bright and showy color. The young shepherd is merry, his sheep skip and frisk: pleasure looks like joy. He is set against the second shepherd, "wild-looking" in a goatskin with a knotted staff and whip (62:5). The contrast is the book's point about luxury: its time is short and sweet, its cost long and bitter (64:4).

a: living in luxury and running wild
p: Tryphē is luxury or soft living; spatalaō, to live self-indulgently, is the word of 1 Timothy 5:6 and James 5:5.
b: Two words carry Similitude 6. Tryphē (verb tryphaō) is luxury, soft or pleasure-seeking living; the site says "luxury" throughout 61-65 so the reader can follow the word. Spatalaō (LSJ: "live softly or in excessive comfort or indulgence," citing 1 Timothy 5:6 and James 5:5) is "running wild." Hermas widens tryphē in 65:5 to any sin done with pleasure.

a: the angel of luxury and deceit
t: An evil angel, or a righteous one?
p: The first shepherd is a bad angel who ruins souls; the second is a righteous angel who punishes.
b: Hermas's world has good and bad angels: Mandate 6 taught that each person has an angel of righteousness and an angel of wickedness (36 (Mandate 6.2)). The angel of luxury and deceit is plainly evil: he "wears out the souls of God's slaves." By contrast, the angel of punishment is "one of the righteous angels" (63:2): harsh, but on God's side. So suffering in this book can be the work of a good angel for the sinner's good, while pleasure can be the work of an evil one.

a: some to death and some to ruin
p: Two outcomes: death (no repentance) and ruin (corrupted, but with hope of renewal).
b: Hermas distinguishes thanatos, "death," from kataphthora, "ruin" or corruption. Death is for those who are torn away "for good" and have spoken evil against God's name; ruin is for those corrupted by luxury but who never blasphemed. "Ruin has hope of some renewal, but death brings destruction forever" (62:4). It is a scale of sin like 1 John 5:16-17 ("There is sin headed toward death").

a: For these there is no repentance that leads to life
p: Those who added to their sins and blasphemed have no repentance. Hermas sets limits to the one repentance.
b: The "repentance that leads to life" (metanoia zōēs, compare Acts 11:18) is closed to those who have "spoken evil against the name of God." The same limit appears in Similitude 8 for the apostates whose sticks are dry and moth-eaten (72:4) and for those who denied the Lord because of business (74:2). Compare Mark 3:29 and Hebrews 6:4-6. Whether a believer can fall away for good is asked on the site's "Where Christians differ" card at Hebrews 6, and whether some sins are "mortal" at 1 John 5.

a: wearing a white goatskin
p: A rough herdsman with a bag, a knotted staff and a whip: the angel of punishment.
b: The second shepherd is dressed as a real herdsman of the hills, in a goatskin, with a bag and a knotted club. Prophets wore rough skins too (Zechariah 13:4; Hebrews 11:37). His staff and whip are for driving sheep through thorns. Hermas is frightened of his look, but the Shepherd explains he is righteous (63:2). The goatskin is white, perhaps a hint of that.

a: a place full of cliffs, thorns and thistles
p: Thorns and thistles: the curse of Genesis 3 and the choking cares of the sower parable.
b: "Thorns and thistles" (akanthai kai triboloi) is the pair of Genesis 3:18 (the cursed ground) and Hebrews 6:8 ("if it puts out thorns and thistles, it fails the test and a curse is not far off"). In Jesus' parable the seed among thorns is "choked by worries and wealth and the pleasures of life" (Luke 8:14). Hermas reverses it: those who chose pleasure are now caught in thorns, so that the pain teaches them.

a: the angel of punishment
p: A righteous angel punishes the wandering, to train them. Hermas sees suffering as God's discipline.
b: The angel of punishment (timōria) is "one of the righteous angels" set over punishment, and those he afflicts are then "handed over" to the Shepherd "for good training" (paideia, 63:6). Compare the teaching of Hebrews 12:5-11 ("whoever the Lord loves, he disciplines," Hebrews 12:6) and Proverbs 3:11-12. Hermas is careful that the punishments are of "everyday life" (63:4): losses, poverty, sickness, unrest, insults. Compare also 1 Corinthians 11:30-32.
orig: ὁ ἄγγελος τῆς τιμωρίας (ho angelos tēs timōrias)

a: The torments belong to everyday life
p: Biōtikai: belonging to ordinary life. The torments are not in hell but in this life.
b: The adjective biōtikai, "to do with daily life," is the word of Luke 21:34 ("the worries of making a living") and 1 Corinthians 6:3-4. The "torments" (basanoi, the word used of the rich man's torment in Luke 16:23) are, in the Shepherd's words, the setbacks of "everyday life" in this world. Hermas speaks of death and of "destruction forever" in the same parable (62:3-4), but these torments of the angel of punishment he places in this life, as God's discipline now.
orig: βιωτικαί εἰσιν αἱ βάσανοι (biōtikai eisin hai basanoi)

a: they blame the Lord
p: When their plans fail, people blame God instead of their deeds, as Proverbs and James warn.
b: "A man's folly turns his road upside down, and then he is furious at the LORD in his heart" (Proverbs 19:3), and James warns that someone tempted "must never say, 'It is God who is tempting me'" (James 1:13). Hermas adds that only when a person repents do his evil deeds "come into his heart" (63:6), so that he sees his suffering as just.

a: he is a righteous judge
p: Lake's margin: the Greek Psalm 7:11 and Psalm 62:12, God pays each according to his deeds.
b: The repentant confess that God "is a righteous judge" (Psalm 7:11, which is Psalm 7:12 in the Greek numbering of Lake's margin: ho theos kritēs dikaios; the site's Psalm 7:11 has "God is a judge who does right") and that each suffered "for his own deeds" (Psalm 62:12: "you pay each person back by what he does"; Romans 2:6). Lake prints both psalms and Matthew 21:22 ("you will receive everything you ask for") in his margin. Praising God's justice in one's own punishment is the attitude of Daniel 9:14 and Nehemiah 9:33.
r: Psalm 7:11; Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; Matthew 21:22; 1 John 3:22; Daniel 9:14

a: an hour of torment has the power of thirty days
p: One hour of pleasure costs thirty days; a day of luxury costs a year. Hermas's point is how long pain is remembered.
b: The numbers are odd (an hour equals thirty days, so a day should equal two years, not one), and Hermas himself does not understand them (65:1). The Shepherd's explanation is psychological, not legal: pleasure is forgotten by the next day, but suffering "leaves long memories" (65:3). The torments being measured are those the Shepherd calls "everyday life" (63:4).

a: Whatever a person does with pleasure
p: Hermas widens luxury to any sin enjoyed: even the angry man's anger and the slanderer's talk.
b: The Shepherd makes "luxury" a word for every sin done for its pleasure: the bad-tempered man "lives in luxury" when he gives his passion its fill, and so do the adulterer, drunkard, slanderer, liar, greedy man and cheat. The list echoes the vice lists of the New Testament (1 Corinthians 6:9-10; Galatians 5:19-21). "Bad-tempered" (oxycholos) is the word of Mandate 5 (33-34). In 65:7 he also allows a good "luxury": delight in doing good.

a: there are also kinds of luxury that save people
p: Not all pleasure is bad: those who delight in doing good "live in luxury" and win life.
b: Hermas is no enemy of joy. Cheerfulness (hilarotēs) is a virtue in Mandate 10 (42), and here the one who does good "carried along by his own pleasure in it" lives in a good kind of luxury. Compare 2 Corinthians 9:7, "God loves a glad giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7), and Psalm 37:4. The harmful kinds win "torments and punishments"; only persisting without repentance wins death.

a: the glorious angel
p: A higher angel who sends the Shepherd and orders Hermas's affliction. Some identify him with Michael or with Christ.
b: "The glorious angel" (ho endoxos angelos) gives orders about Hermas and has handed him over to the Shepherd (66:5). In Similitude 8 the "glorious angel of the Lord, very tall" (67:2) is explained as Michael (69:3); in Similitude 9 a "glorious man" is the Son of God (89:8 (Similitude 9.12.8)). Lake's English note on 69:3: "in Sim. ix. he is the Son of God"; this, with what Similitude 9 says of the Son and the Spirit, "makes it very hard to reconstruct the Christology of Hermas." Harnack says it is not certain whether Hermas identifies the Spirit-Son with the chief archangel.

a: you, the head of the household
p: In Roman law the father ruled the household, and its fortunes and troubles were his.
b: Hermas is the kephalē tou oikou, "head of the house." A Roman father had authority over his wife, children and slaves, and the household's property was his. So affliction that falls on him (losses, illness) falls on all of them. The angel uses this to bring the household to repentance. In Vision 1 Hermas was blamed for not correcting his children (3:1 (Vision 1.3.1)).

a: The one who repents must torment his own soul
p: The angel says no: the penitent must suffer and humble himself first. A key text in the history of penance.
b: Here Hermas teaches that repentance is followed by a time of suffering and humbling before God's "healing." The penitent must "torment his own soul" (basanisai tēn heautou psychēn), be humble, and bear afflictions; then God "will surely have compassion." Lake sees in Hermas "the beginning of the Catholic doctrine of penance." Compare 1 John 1:9 and Luke 18:13-14, where forgiveness follows confession. Lake's English has "torture his own soul" for basanisai. See the variant on "at once." On the one repentance, see 31:6 (Mandate 4.3.6).

a: Not at all.
p: The Shepherd denies that the sins are forgiven at once, not that they are forgiven.
b: The Greek is ou pantelōs; Lake's English has "By no means." The denial answers the question just asked: are the sins of those who repent forgiven "at once"? The answer is no, not at once, and the rest of the verse says what comes first: humbling, affliction, and then God's "healing." Forgiveness itself is not denied (66:5; 77:3). On the word "at once," see the variant.

a: shown the suffering ahead of time
p: Hermas is told to be thankful that he knows beforehand, so he can bear it.
b: Knowing trouble before it comes is a gift: so Jesus tells his disciples, "I have said these things to you so that you will not be tripped up" (John 16:1), and Paul tells the Thessalonians that he had told them beforehand they would suffer (1 Thessalonians 3:4). The Shepherd also promises to ask the punishing angel to afflict Hermas "more lightly" (66:6), a picture of angels interceding.

a: a great willow tree that covered plains and mountains
p: A tree over all the earth sheltering all who are called: the law of God, which is the Son of God (69:2).
b: The world tree that shelters the nations is an old image: Nebuchadnezzar's tree in Daniel 4:10-12, the cedar of Ezekiel 17:22-24 and 31:3-9, the mustard plant of Matthew 13:31-32 whose branches shelter the birds. Hermas's tree is a willow, which grows readily from cut sticks and loves water (68:7). Its shade covers "all who have been called by the name of the Lord." In the explanation the tree is "God's law ... given to the whole world," and "this law is the Son of God" (69:2).

a: called by the name of the Lord
p: Believers bear the Lord's name, given in baptism, as in James 2:7.
b: Hermas speaks of those "called in the name of the Lord" (en onomati kyriou) and later of "the Lord's name, which was pronounced over them" (72:4), the phrase of James 2:7: "Don't they insult the good name that was pronounced over you?" (James 2:7). Lake prints that verse in his margin at 72:4. In the Hebrew Bible God's name "called over" a people or place marks it as his (Deuteronomy 28:10; Amos 9:12).

a: He handed them small sticks, about a cubit long
p: A cubit was the length of a forearm, about a foot and a half.
b: A cubit (pēchys) was the length from elbow to fingertip, about 18 inches (45 cm). The angel cuts small sticks (rhabdia) from the willow and gives one to each person. The test of the sticks recalls Numbers 17, where each tribe's staff (rhabdos in the Greek) is laid before the LORD and Aaron's "sprouted! It had brought out buds, burst into blossom and ripened almonds" (Numbers 17:8).

a: that tree was whole, just as I had seen it before
p: So many branches cut, yet the tree is whole: the law (the Son) is given to all and is not diminished.
b: Hermas is puzzled (67:4; 69:1), and the Shepherd's answer is the identity of the tree: the law that is the Son of God, preached to the ends of the earth (69:2). Giving it to everyone takes nothing from it. Hermas does not develop the point, but the tree's wholeness is meant to be a wonder.

a: dry and eaten as if by moths
p: The sticks come back in many states, from dry and moth-eaten to green with fruit. Each is a kind of believer.
b: The sticks are handed back in thirteen conditions: dry and moth-eaten (67:6), dry (67:7), half dry (67:8), half dry with cracks (67:9), green with cracks (67:10), half and half (67:11), two-thirds green (67:12), two-thirds dry (67:13), green with dry tips and cracks (67:14), mostly dry (67:15), green as received (67:16), green with shoots (67:17), green with shoots and fruit (67:18). The Shepherd explains them in 72-76, almost in this order. The scale runs from apostates to martyrs.

a: Most of the crowd handed in sticks like this
p: Hermas's church is not mostly corrupt: the largest group returns the stick green, just as received.
b: The largest group (to pleion meros tou ochlou) returns the stick unchanged, and the angel rejoices. Hermas is often read as a stern book, but here the majority have kept what they received (69:8: "reverent and righteous people"). The book's warnings fall on minorities: the double-minded, the quarrelsome, those tangled in business, the rich who have drifted to the nations.

a: crowns were brought that looked as if they were made of palm leaves
p: Those with fruit-bearing sticks are crowned and dressed in white: the martyrs (69:6), as in Revelation 7.
b: Palm branches greet a victory in 1 Maccabees 13:51 ("he entered it with praise and palm branches") and a king in John 12:13. In Revelation the great crowd stands "dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands" (Revelation 7:9), and the one who stays faithful to death receives "the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10). Hermas puts the palm crown on those who "wrestled with the devil and defeated him ... who suffered for the law" (69:6).

a: He gave them seals
p: The seal in Hermas is baptism (93:3-4). Here the entrants into the tower receive a seal.
b: The Greek sphragis, "seal," is the site's word for the mark of ownership God puts on his people (Ephesians 1:13; Revelation 7:3). In Similitude 9 Hermas says plainly that "the seal is the water" of baptism (93:4 (Similitude 9.16.4)), which part 093-114 treats. In 72:3 those who "received the seal, and broke it" are baptized believers who sinned; they are to receive a seal again from the Shepherd. Whether that second seal is a rite or a figure for repentance is not said.

a: into the walls
p: The tower is the church; the walls around it are a lower place for those who repented late.
b: The tower stands for the church, as in Vision 3 (10-15) and Similitude 9 (78-110). Here there are also "walls" around it, a lower dwelling for some who repent (72:6; 73:3). The scale is a scale of honor or nearness, not of saved and lost: "Those of them who have repented more slowly will live in the walls" (73:3). Similitude 9 retells the tower at length.

a: I will test them at the altar
p: The angel will examine anyone who slips past: probably a heavenly altar, as in Revelation.
b: Epi to thysiastērion, "at the altar," is unexplained. Revelation has an altar in heaven (Revelation 6:9; 8:3-5), and a heavenly judgment scene may be meant, with the angel making his own examination; or the church's own altar. Hermas gives no explanation, and the Shepherd does not refer to it again.

a: its kind loves life
p: Willow cuttings root easily in wet ground: a fact every farmer knew.
b: Willows (itea) root from cut sticks pushed into wet ground, which is why the Shepherd hopes that even dry sticks will live if planted and watered. The adjective philozōos, "life-loving," is used again in 72:1 for the lesson: "I told you that this tree loves life. Do you see how many repented and were saved?" Isaiah 44:4 pictures the Spirit's blessing as plants springing up "like poplars beside running streams" (Isaiah 44:4).

a: wants all who received branches from this tree to live
p: Lake's margin: 1 Timothy 2:4, God wants everyone to be saved.
b: "The one who created this tree wants all ... to live." Lake prints 1 Timothy 2:4 in the margin: "He wants everyone to be saved and to arrive at full knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). Compare Ezekiel 18:23, 32 and 2 Peter 3:9, which Lake prints at 77:1. The Shepherd's own attitude matches: "no one will find that I was careless" (68:7).

a: this law is the Son of God
p: Hermas identifies the law given to the world with the Son of God, preached to the ends of the earth.
b: Hermas calls the Son of God the law itself. The Epistle of Barnabas speaks of "the new law of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Epistle of Barnabas 2:6), and Isaiah 2:3 of the law that goes out from Zion ("from Zion comes teaching", the Hebrew word being torah). On what "the law" means for Hermas, see Lake's note at 69:6. The "preaching" (kērygma) of the Son to "the ends of the earth" recalls Matthew 24:14 and Acts 1:8.
orig: ὁ δὲ νόμος οὗτος υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐστ' κηρυχθεὶς εἰς τὰ πέρατα τῆς γῆς
r: Isaiah 2:3; Epistle of Barnabas 2:6; Matthew 24:14; Acts 1:8; Galatians 6:2; 59:3

a: The great and glorious angel is Michael
t: Michael, the angel over the people
p: The angel who gives and checks the law is Michael. Is he the Son, or an angel under the Son?
b: In Daniel, Michael is "the great prince who stands guard over the sons of your people" (Daniel 12:1). Hermas makes him the angel "who has authority over this people and steers them," who "puts the law into the hearts of those who believe," in the words of Jeremiah 31:33 ("on their hearts I will write it"). Lake's note: "in Sim. ix. he [the glorious angel] is the Son of God"; this, with what Similitude 9 says of the Son and the Spirit, makes Hermas's Christology "very hard to reconstruct." The text leaves open whether Michael is an angel serving under the Son, who is the tree and the law, or the Son himself pictured as the chief angel; Harnack writes that it is "not certain" which (see the chapter page). Schaff counts Michael as chief of Hermas's six first angels.
r: Daniel 12:1; Daniel 10:13; Jude 1:9; Revelation 12:7; Jeremiah 31:33; Galatians 3:19

a: he left under my authority, for repentance
p: Those who kept the law are under Michael; those who broke it are given to the angel of repentance.
b: The Shepherd's whole office is here: "All who broke the law ... he left under my authority, for repentance." Those who kept it stay under Michael's own authority. The church is pictured as two groups, the faithful and the penitent, each under an angel. Hermas describes no rite for the second group.

a: All who wrestled with the devil and defeated him
p: The martyrs are wrestlers who beat the devil, as in Ephesians 6:12.
b: The verb antepalaisan, "wrestled against," is from the wrestling ring; Paul says "our wrestling match is not against blood and flesh" but against spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12). Lake's English note on 69:6-7: "'Suffer' means 'suffer a death of martyrdom,' and the law means the Christian rule of life, not (as in the N.T.) the Jewish Law." Victors in the games were crowned; so the martyrs are crowned with palm (68:1). Compare Revelation 12:11 and 4 Maccabees 17:11-16, where the Jewish martyrs are athletes.

a: afflicted for the law, but did not suffer
p: A second rank: those persecuted but not killed, who did not deny. Later called confessors.
b: Those whose sticks have shoots but no fruit "were afflicted for the law, but did not suffer" (did not die) and "did not deny." Later Christians called such people "confessors": those who confessed Christ under persecution and survived. They too go into the tower, with seals (68:2). Hermas's ranks show a church that had known persecution in Rome. The Visions speak of a "great affliction" that is coming (6:7 (Vision 2.2.7)), and 1 Clement 5-6 remembers the Roman martyrs.

a: Tie on a towel
p: Hermas ties on a towel to serve the Shepherd, as slaves did at table, and as Jesus did in John 13.
b: Lake's English note: "The exact meaning of ōmolinon is apparently 'made of undressed flax,' but it came to mean merely a towel." LSJ gives ōmolinos "made of raw flax." Slaves tied a towel around the waist to serve; Jesus "took a towel and fastened it around himself" to wash the disciples' feet (John 13:4), and the returning master of Luke 12:37 "will tie up his own robe ... and serve them." Here the human seer serves the angel. The towel is "made of sackcloth," the cloth of mourning and repentance.

a: They all stood in their groups
p: Tagma, a rank or company, often of soldiers. Lake: "stations."
b: Tagma is an ordered company, a military unit, or a rank; Paul uses it of the order of the resurrection ("each in his own rank," 1 Corinthians 15:23). Lake's English uses "stations." The site says "groups," since Hermas means the people sorted by the state of their sticks. The text of 70:6 about who stands where is, in Lake's words, "obscure and probably corrupt."

a: some with their own groups and others by themselves
p: Lake: some were sent back to their original group and others moved apart, but "the text is obscure and probably corrupt."
b: Lake's English note on this sentence: "This must mean that some were sent back to their original place, others were moved aside. But the text is obscure and probably corrupt." The Plain English Translation renders Lake's Greek as it stands: he ordered them each to stand apart, some with their own groups and others by themselves.
orig: τοὺς μὲν πρὸς τὰ ἴδια τάγματα, τοὺς δὲ χωρίς

a: they had all been changed and had put away their cracks
p: Planted and watered, the cracked sticks come back green: repentance really changes people.
b: The planting and watering in 68:8 is the time given for repentance, and now the results are counted. Some sticks are better than before, some the same, some worse. Hermas's point is hopeful: "this tree loves life" (72:1). The water may suggest baptism or the Spirit (Isaiah 44:3), but the Shepherd explains it only as the gift of repentance.

a: He gave a spirit to those who were worthy of repentance
p: Repentance is God's gift, and he gives it to those he foresees will repent truly.
b: Hermas says both that God "gave a spirit" to the worthy (72:1) and that he "gave repentance" to those whose hearts he saw would become pure (72:2). That repentance is a gift is a New Testament idea (Acts 5:31; 11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). That God withholds it from those he foresees would repent "in hypocrisy" is Hermas's answer to why not all repent. How God's foreknowledge and human choice relate here is left open, and readers from different traditions draw different conclusions from it.

a: received the seal, and broke it
p: The baptized who sinned have broken their seal; they may receive a seal again from the Shepherd.
b: The verb thlaō means to crush or break (Lake's text has the perfect tethlakotes). A broken seal on a document or a jar meant tampering: the baptized who sin have "broken" the mark of baptism. Hermas hopes they will "receive a seal from you," the angel of repentance. Whether this means a second baptism, a rite of reconciliation, or simply repentance pictured as a seal, is not said; part 093-114 treats the seal of baptism (93-94).
orig: εἰληφότες τὴν σφραγῖδα καὶ τεθλακότες αὐτήν

a: the deserters and betrayers of the church
p: Some had left the church and some had betrayed its members to the authorities.
b: Apostatai are deserters, those who left the faith; prodotai, "betrayers," are probably informers who handed fellow Christians over to the authorities, as Jesus warned would happen (Matthew 24:10). The Plain English Translation keeps "betrayers of the church" without deciding the details. For these, "life has left": the dry, moth-eaten sticks stay dry.

a: brought in strange teachings
p: Hypocrites with strange teachings who would not let sinners repent: probably rigorists.
b: These teachers "would not let them repent" (mē aphientes metanoein), especially those who had sinned. Hermas thus attacks people who taught that there is no repentance after baptism: the view Lake says was held in Hermas's circle ("if they fell they could not again obtain forgiveness"). Hebrews 13:9 warns against "teachings of many colors and foreign origin," with the same adjective xenai. Hermas's own teaching of a second chance is set against theirs, and even for them he holds out hope.

a: For they are neither alive nor dead
p: The double-minded are half-dry sticks, like the lukewarm church of Revelation 3.
b: The half-dry stick is the double-minded person (dipsychos), "neither alive nor dead." The picture is close to the church of Laodicea, "neither cold nor hot" (Revelation 3:15), and to the church of Sardis: "You have a name for being alive, but you are dead" (Revelation 3:1). James 1:8 calls the double-minded man "never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:8).

a: always split into factions
p: Dichostasia, splitting into parties: a vice in Paul's list (Galatians 5:20) and in Hermas's church.
b: Dichostateō, "to stand apart, to split," and the noun dichostasia (73:5) are the words of Galatians 5:20 and Romans 16:17. Hermas joins faction to slander: those who talk against others are never at peace. Lake prints 1 Thessalonians 5:13 in the margin, "Keep the peace among yourselves" (1 Thessalonians 5:13). The Roman church had also written 1 Clement to Corinth about a split in that church (1 Clement 46:5).

a: jealousy among themselves about first places
p: Good believers who quarrel over rank and glory, like the disciples in Mark 9 and 10.
b: Prōteia, "first places," are the seats of honor. The disciples debated "which of them ranked highest" (Mark 9:34), and James and John asked for the seats at Jesus' right and left (Mark 10:37). Third John names "Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them" (3 John 1:9). Hermas, a Roman Christian whose Visions speak to "those who lead the church" (17:7 (Vision 3.9.7)), sees the same rivalry in his own congregation. The cure is in the commandments: "patience and ... a person's humility" (73:6).

a: tangled up in business
p: The word of 2 Timothy 2:4: the soldier does not get tangled in everyday business.
b: The perfect participle empephyrmenoi means "mixed up in, tangled in." Compare 2 Timothy 2:4, "No one serving in the army gets tangled up in the business of everyday life" (2 Timothy 2:4), with the same noun pragmateiai, "business affairs." Such people "do not hold on to the saints" (mē kollōmenoi, "stick to"): they drift from the church's life. Similitude 4 gave the same warning (53:5-7).

a: the saints
p: Hoi hagioi, God's holy people: the members of the church.
b: The site renders hoi hagioi "the saints," with the gloss "God's holy people," as in Paul's letters (Romans 1:7). In Hermas the saints are the believing community as a whole, not a group of especially holy people.

a: those who denied in various ways
p: Hermas does not say how they denied. The phrase covers more than one way of giving up the faith.
b: Hermas does not list the "various denials" (poikilai arnēseis). In 50:5 he warned that property tempts a believer to "deny his law," and in 74:2 business led some to deny the Lord; Peter's denial in the Gospels is the classic case (Matthew 26:69-75). Many of the deniers here repented and went into the tower.

a: these lost their life for good
p: Eis telos: completely, to the end. Hermas uses it for those beyond repentance.
b: The phrase eis telos, "to the end, completely," marks the hopeless cases in Hermas: those torn away from God "for good" (62:3), "lost to God for good" (72:4), who "fell away for good" (74:2, 74:5), and who lived with the nations "for good" (75:3). The Plain English Translation keeps one rendering so the reader can follow the line between those who can still repent and those who cannot.

a: grew rich and became respected among the nations
p: Some believers who became wealthy and honored in pagan society drifted away from the church.
b: "The nations" (ta ethnē) are the pagan world. These Christians kept the faith in name but "lived together with the nations" and found that way "more pleasant." Roman social life (patronage, banquets, guilds, civic offices) was full of pagan religion, and a rising Christian had to choose how far to take part. Hermas's verdict is mild for those who "did not fall away from God" but did not do "the works of faith": many repented. Compare James 2:14-17 and 1 Timothy 6:17.

a: These were counted with the nations
p: Those who lived like pagans for good share the pagans' fate (53:4).
b: "Counted with the nations" (meta tōn ethnōn elogisthēsan) means they share the fate of the nations in Similitude 4: the nations "will be burned because they did not know the one who created them" (53:4). Compare Luke 22:37, "And he was counted with the lawless" (Luke 22:37), quoting Isaiah 53:12, with the same verb in the Greek.

a: It will be hard for any of them to die
p: These good people with small faults will hardly be lost: spiritual death is unlikely for them.
b: Dyskolōs ... apothaneitai, "with difficulty will die." "Die" in this chapter means to be lost (73:3: "will surely die"). The Shepherd means that people who were always good, and who only made small splits, will hardly be lost. It is a note of mercy in a long list.

a: those who only believed, but did the works of lawlessness
p: Believers in name who did lawless deeds, yet welcomed God's slaves into their homes: they repented at once.
b: "Only believed" (pisteusantes monon) recalls James 2:24: "it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (James 2:24). These people did wrong, but they "bore the name gladly" and "gladly welcomed God's slaves into their homes," hospitality that Hermas counts in their favor (compare Matthew 25:35; Hebrews 13:2). Hearing of repentance, they took it at once. Whether faith alone saves is asked on the site's "Where Christians differ" cards at Romans 3 and James 2.

a: the calling that came through his Son
p: God is patient because he wants the calling made through his Son to be saved. Lake's margin: 2 Peter 3:9.
b: "The calling" (hē klēsis) is God's call to the church through the Son, and here almost the church itself: God wants it "saved." Lake prints 2 Peter 3:9 in the margin: "he bears patiently with you. He does not want any to be lost, but wants all to arrive at repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). This is one of the few places in the book where the Son is named as the one through whom God acts in history; compare 58:3, "the commandments he gave his people through his Son."
orig: τὴν κλῆσιν τὴν γενομένην διὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ

a: will receive healing from the Lord for their former sins
p: Forgiveness for past sins, on three conditions: whole-hearted repentance, no new sins, no double-mindedness.
b: The Similitude ends with the book's message in brief: those who repent "with their whole heart," clean themselves, "add nothing more to their sins," and are not double-minded will be healed of "their former sins." Those who add to their sins condemn themselves. Lake summarizes Hermas's teaching as "for sin after baptism there was still the possibility of forgiveness for those who repented, though this repentance would not avail more than once." Compare Hebrews 10:26 and 1 John 2:1.

a: I will show you the rest in a few days
p: The Shepherd promises more: Similitude 9, the longest part of the book, retells the tower.
b: The closing line points ahead to Similitude 9 (78-110), where Hermas is taken to Arcadia and shown the tower again in full. Part 078-092 begins there.
